questions.stem: An organism's ecological niche is best described as:
options: its role in the ecosystem, including what it eats, where it lives and how it interacts
the physical place where it lives, such as a hollow log or a rock pool on a rocky shore
the total number of individuals of its species living in one part of the ecosystem
the group of other species that compete with it for the same food in its habitat
questions.explanation: A niche includes the species' habitat, food, activity times, tolerances and interactions with other species: its whole way of life. The physical place alone is its habitat, which is only part of the niche.

questions.stem: Compared with a species that has a narrow niche, a species with a broad niche:
options: always outcompetes every other species, so it never shares resources with any others
lives only in one type of ecosystem, so it is limited to a very small geographic range overall
can use a wide range of foods and habitats, so it copes better with environmental change
depends on a single food source, so it is more vulnerable when that resource declines
questions.explanation: A broad niche means wide tolerances and many resources, so the species can switch when one resource fails. Dependence on a single food source describes a narrow niche.

questions.stem: Two species of honeyeater feed on nectar in the same forest. One feeds in the canopy and the other in the understorey shrubs, and both populations persist. This is best explained by:
options: resource partitioning, which reduces interspecific competition between them
mutualism, because each species benefits directly from the other species' feeding
intraspecific competition, which forces each species into a separate layer
parasitism, because one species takes nectar that the other one has found
questions.explanation: When two species divide a shared resource by feeding in different places or at different times, their niches overlap less and interspecific competition falls, allowing both to coexist. Intraspecific competition is between members of the same species.

questions.stem: If two species have exactly the same niche in the same area, ecologists predict that:
options: the two species will interbreed and form a single new species over time
neither species will be affected, because niches never limit populations
one species will outcompete the other, which will decline or be excluded
both species will increase because they can share all resources equally
questions.explanation: Two species cannot occupy an identical niche indefinitely (the competitive exclusion principle): the better competitor eventually excludes the other locally. Sharing resources equally without any effect is not what is observed.

questions.stem: Two male Tasmanian devils fighting over a carcass is an example of:
options: predation
commensalism
intraspecific competition
interspecific competition
questions.explanation: Intraspecific competition occurs between members of the same species for the same resource, here food. Interspecific competition would be between different species, such as a devil and a quoll.

questions.stem: Why is intraspecific competition usually more intense than interspecific competition?
options: Members of the same species have identical resource needs
Members of the same species never live in the same habitat
Different species always need far more resources than one
Different species can never use the same food or shelter
questions.explanation: Individuals of one species need exactly the same food, shelter and mates, so their niches overlap completely. Different species overlap only partly, so competition between them is usually less intense.

questions.stem: Introduced European wasps and native birds both feed on insects in a Tasmanian forest. This relationship is:
options: mutualism, because both groups benefit from removing the insect pests
commensalism, because the wasps benefit and the birds are unaffected
interspecific competition, which can reduce food available to the birds
intraspecific competition, as both groups feed on the same type of food
questions.explanation: Different species using the same limited resource are in interspecific competition, which can lower the food supply for each. Mutualism requires each species to benefit from the other, not from a shared food.

questions.stem: In which relationship does one species benefit while the other is harmed but usually not killed straight away?
options: Commensalism
Competition
Parasitism
Mutualism
questions.explanation: A parasite lives on or in a host and obtains food from it, harming the host but usually not killing it quickly. In mutualism both benefit; in commensalism one benefits and the other is unaffected.

questions.stem: Mosses and ferns grow on the trunks of myrtle beech in Tasmanian rainforest, gaining access to light without taking nutrients from the tree. This is:
options: mutualism
predation
commensalism
parasitism
questions.explanation: Epiphytes use the tree only for support and better light, so they benefit while the tree is largely unaffected, which is commensalism. They do not take water or nutrients from the tree, so it is not parasitism.

questions.stem: Reef-building corals host algae (zooxanthellae) in their tissues. The algae get shelter and nutrients, and the coral gets sugars from photosynthesis. This relationship is:
options: mutualism
commensalism
parasitism
competition
questions.explanation: Both partners benefit, so this is mutualism. When stressed corals expel the algae (bleaching), they lose most of their food supply, showing how much each depends on the other.

questions.stem: Mistletoe attaches to the branches of a eucalypt and draws water and minerals from it. Heavy mistletoe infestations can weaken the tree. Mistletoe is acting as a:
options: parasite
predator
mutualist
decomposer
questions.explanation: Mistletoe gains water and minerals from its host and harms it without killing it quickly, which is parasitism. A predator kills and eats its prey.

questions.stem: Which symbols correctly summarise mutualism, commensalism and parasitism (benefit +, harm -, no effect 0)?
options: Mutualism +/-, commensalism +/0, parasitism +/+
Mutualism +/+, commensalism +/0, parasitism +/-
Mutualism +/0, commensalism +/+, parasitism +/-
Mutualism +/+, commensalism +/-, parasitism +/0
questions.explanation: In mutualism both species benefit, in commensalism one benefits and the other is unaffected, and in parasitism one benefits at the other's expense. Predation is also +/- but the prey is killed.

questions.stem: The koala feeds almost entirely on the leaves of a limited range of eucalypt species. It is best described as a:
options: specialist with a narrow niche
generalist with a broad niche
specialist with a broad niche
generalist with a narrow niche
questions.explanation: A specialist depends on a narrow range of resources, giving it a narrow niche. Generalists, such as the common brushtail possum, eat a wide range of foods.

questions.stem: After a large bushfire destroys most of a forest's eucalypts, which species is most likely to recover its numbers fastest?
options: A specialist bird that nests only in old eucalypt hollows
A specialist insect that feeds only on the nectar of eucalypts
A generalist omnivore that eats plants, insects and carrion
A specialist herbivore that eats one species of eucalypt
questions.explanation: Generalists can switch to whatever food remains, so they tolerate disturbance better. Each specialist depends on a resource the fire has removed, so they decline sharply and recover slowly.

questions.stem: Which of these is a characteristic of a population rather than of an individual?
options: Heart rate
Diet
Age structure
Body mass
questions.explanation: Populations have properties such as size, density, distribution pattern, age structure, sex ratio and growth rate. Body mass and heart rate belong to individuals.

questions.stem: Seabirds such as short-tailed shearwaters nest in dense colonies on certain coastal sites but are absent from the land between them. This distribution pattern is:
options: even
clumped
uniform
random
questions.explanation: A clumped distribution occurs where resources, such as suitable burrowing ground, are patchy or where animals gather socially. Uniform distribution results from competition or territoriality spacing individuals evenly.

questions.stem: An age-structure diagram for a wallaby population shows very few young and many old individuals. What does this suggest?
options: The population is stable because births exactly equal deaths
The population has a high birth rate and a very low death rate
The population is likely to decline because recruitment is low
The population is likely to grow rapidly because adults are many
questions.explanation: Few juveniles means few individuals will reach breeding age to replace the older animals as they die, so the population is likely to shrink. A growing population has a broad base of young individuals.

questions.stem: A population grows when:
options: births plus immigration exceed deaths plus emigration
births plus emigration exceed deaths plus immigration
deaths plus immigration exceed births plus emigration
births exceed immigration, regardless of deaths
questions.explanation: Population change = (births + immigration) - (deaths + emigration). Births and immigration add individuals; deaths and emigration remove them.

questions.stem: A population of 400 pademelons has 120 births, 60 deaths, 10 immigrants and 30 emigrants in a year. What is its size at the end of the year?
questions.explanation: Change = (120 + 10) - (60 + 30) = 130 - 90 = 40, so the population becomes 440. Ignoring migration altogether gives 460, and counting only births gives 520.

questions.stem: A population of 2000 has a birth rate of 15 per 100 per year and a death rate of 9 per 100 per year, with no migration. What is the expected population after one year?
questions.explanation: Births = 0.15 x 2000 = 300 and deaths = 0.09 x 2000 = 180, a net gain of 120, giving 2120. Counting births without deaths gives 2300.

questions.stem: Carrying capacity is the:
options: total number of different species that live in an ecosystem at once
maximum population an environment can support sustainably over time
largest number of offspring a single female can produce in her life
fastest rate at which a population can grow when resources are unlimited
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity (K) is the largest population size the environment's resources can sustain over the long term. The fastest possible growth rate with unlimited resources is the biotic potential.

questions.stem: Which of these is a density-independent limiting factor?
options: A disease that spreads faster as animals become more crowded
Competition for nesting sites that increases as numbers of birds rise
Predation that increases as prey become easier to find
A severe flood that drowns animals regardless of population size
questions.explanation: Density-independent factors such as floods, fires and droughts affect a population whatever its density. Disease, competition and predation usually intensify as density increases, so they are density-dependent.

questions.stem: Environmental resistance refers to:
options: all the limiting factors that together prevent a population reaching its biotic potential
the ability of an ecosystem to return to its original state after a disturbance has passed
the resistance of a species to a pesticide that develops after many years of exposure
the tendency of a population to keep growing once it has passed its carrying capacity
questions.explanation: Environmental resistance is the combined effect of factors such as limited food, space, predation and disease that slow growth below the maximum possible rate. The ability to return after disturbance is resilience.

questions.stem: A population of deer on an island overshoots its carrying capacity and overgrazes its food plants. What is the most likely long-term result?
options: A rise in carrying capacity, because more deer means more food is found each day
A population crash, and a lower carrying capacity until the vegetation recovers
Continued growth, because overgrazing increases plant productivity on the island
A stable population at the original carrying capacity, with no fall in numbers
questions.explanation: Overshooting damages the resource base, so food runs short and the population crashes. Carrying capacity can stay reduced until the damaged vegetation regrows.

questions.stem: A J-shaped population growth curve shows:
options: a population that stays at a constant size for its whole recorded history
regular rises and falls of a prey population that follow its predator numbers
exponential growth with no limiting factors, often followed by a sudden crash
growth that slows and levels off as the population reaches carrying capacity
questions.explanation: A J curve is exponential growth when resources are effectively unlimited. Without a gradual levelling, it usually ends in a crash when resources run out. Levelling off at carrying capacity is an S curve.

questions.stem: On an S-shaped (logistic) growth curve, why does the growth rate slow as the population nears carrying capacity?
options: The birth rate rises sharply while the death rate stays exactly the same
Individuals emigrate only when the population is very small
Predators disappear once the population has reached its peak
Environmental resistance increases as resources per individual decline
questions.explanation: As numbers grow, competition for food and space, disease and predation increase, so births fall and deaths rise until they balance at carrying capacity. A rising birth rate would speed growth, not slow it.

questions.stem: European rabbits released in Australia in the nineteenth century spread rapidly across huge areas. Their early growth most closely followed:
options: an S curve, because food was scarce from the moment they arrived
a J curve, because there were few predators or diseases and abundant food
an S curve, because native predators immediately held their numbers stable
a J curve, because the rabbits had already reached carrying capacity
questions.explanation: With plentiful food and few effective predators or diseases, rabbit numbers grew exponentially. An S curve shows growth limited by environmental resistance from early on.

questions.stem: A yeast culture is grown in a flask of sugar solution. Numbers rise slowly, then rapidly, then level off, and finally fall. The final fall is best explained by:
options: the food supply running out and waste products such as alcohol building up
predators entering the flask once the yeast population had levelled off at K
immigration of yeast cells from outside the flask during the final stage
the carrying capacity rising steadily after the population levelled off
questions.explanation: A closed flask has a fixed supply of sugar and no removal of wastes, so after levelling off the yeast deplete food and are poisoned by their own alcohol, causing decline. A closed flask has no immigration or predators.

questions.stem: In a typical predator-prey graph, the predator population peaks:
options: shortly before the prey population peaks
only when the prey population is lowest
shortly after the prey population peaks
at exactly the same time as the prey peaks
questions.explanation: Predators increase after prey become abundant, because more food means more predator offspring survive. Their peak therefore lags behind the prey peak, and as prey fall, predators follow.

questions.stem: In a long-term study, numbers of a native owl and its rodent prey rise and fall in cycles. Which observation would best support the idea that the owls are regulating the rodents?
options: Rodent numbers fall at the same time every year, regardless of owl numbers
Owl numbers rise after a drought kills most of the rodents in the study area
Rodent numbers fall soon after owl numbers rise, and recover after owls decline
Owl numbers stay constant while rodent numbers rise and fall every two or three years
questions.explanation: If predation controls the prey, prey should decline after predators increase and recover when predators fall: a lagged, linked cycle. Rodent falls unrelated to owl numbers would suggest other factors, such as weather, are responsible.

questions.stem: Why is the predator population usually smaller than the prey population in a predator-prey graph?
options: Predators are always larger animals, so fewer can fit into any habitat
Prey feed on predators when prey numbers are high, keeping them low
Less energy is available at the higher trophic level the predator occupies
Predators reproduce faster, so they quickly run short of suitable breeding sites
questions.explanation: Only about 10% of the energy in prey becomes predator biomass, so an area supports far fewer predators than prey. Predators generally reproduce more slowly than their prey, not faster.

questions.stem: In a range of tolerance diagram, the optimal zone is where:
options: the abiotic factor allows maximum growth, reproduction and population size
organisms survive but grow and reproduce poorly because of physiological stress
organisms cannot survive at all because the factor is beyond their limits
the abiotic factor changes the fastest throughout the course of a day
questions.explanation: The optimal zone is the part of the range where conditions suit the species best and the population is largest. On either side lie zones of physiological stress, then zones of intolerance where the species cannot survive.

questions.stem: Trout numbers in a river are low in a stretch where summer water temperature is near the upper limit they can survive. This stretch lies in the trout's:
options: zone of maximum growth and reproduction
zone of physiological stress
optimal zone
zone of intolerance
questions.explanation: The fish survive but in reduced numbers because conditions stress them, which defines the zone of physiological stress. In the zone of intolerance they would be absent altogether.

questions.stem: A shellfish lives in an estuary where salinity ranges widely. Laboratory tests show its optimal salinity is 25 to 30 parts per thousand and it dies below 10 or above 40. At a site where salinity is usually 12, you would expect:
options: no individuals at all, because the site is outside the optimal zone
the largest population in the estuary, because salinity is lowest there
a small population of stressed individuals with low reproduction
a large population, because the site is within the survival range
questions.explanation: A salinity of 12 is within the tolerance range but well below the optimum, so the site is in a zone of physiological stress: few, stressed individuals. Lying outside the optimal zone does not mean the species is absent, only that it is limited.

questions.stem: A species has a wide range of tolerance for temperature but a narrow range for salinity. Which factor is more likely to limit its distribution?
options: Neither, because tolerance ranges have no effect on where species are found
Salinity, because small changes in it take the species outside its tolerance
Temperature, because a wide range means it is more sensitive to small changes
Temperature, because every species is limited by temperature above all else
questions.explanation: The factor with the narrowest tolerance range is most likely to limit where a species can live, because even small changes exceed its limits. A wide range indicates the species copes well with variation in that factor.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a population?
options: All the different species living and interacting in a particular area together
All the living things in an area together with their non-living surroundings
All the individuals of one species, wherever they are found in the world
All the individuals of one species living in a particular area at the same time
questions.explanation: A population is one species in one area at one time. All the interacting species form a community, and a community with its abiotic surroundings is an ecosystem.

questions.stem: A large carnivorous marsupial hunts and kills wallabies for food. The relationship between the carnivore and the wallabies is:
options: predation, which benefits the predator and kills the prey
parasitism, which benefits one species and kills the other
mutualism, as both species benefit from the interaction
commensalism, because the predator benefits and the prey is unaffected
questions.explanation: In predation one animal kills and eats another. Parasites usually harm but do not quickly kill their host, which distinguishes parasitism from predation.
